periods.activity_title: First Read: Meeting the Farmer and the Panchayat

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the story setting: a small farming village, a hardworking farmer, and a cunning neighbour. Students predict what a 'Panchayat' might be and share ideas briefly.
Teacher reads the full narrative aloud from Textbook pp.91–104, using distinct voices for the farmer, neighbour, and Panchayat chief. Students follow along in their copies.
Students re-read the key passage describing the neighbour's claim and the Panchayat scene (pp.91–95) in pairs, one partner reading while the other listens and follows.
Class discussion: teacher asks students to recall — in their own words — what the farmer bought, what dispute arose, and who was called to resolve it. Responses are oral; no writing yet.
Teacher summarises the story arc aloud, naming the three key moments: the purchase, the dispute, and the Panchayat meeting. Students close books.

periods.teacher_notes: The story turns on a clever legal trick, so linger on the neighbour's claim ('I sold the well, not the water') and let students react before moving on. Watch for students who confuse 'Panchayat' with any general assembly — clarify it is a formal village council with authority to settle disputes.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion: Let us Think Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.95): answer four questions about the farmer, his upset, and the Panchayat's judgment.

time_bands.activity: Students re-read the Panchayat meeting section silently (pp.92–95) to refresh the events in their minds before answering questions.

Let us Think — A. (p.95): teacher poses question 1 ('Why did the farmer buy the well?') and question 2 ('Why did the farmer become upset?') to the class. Students respond orally; teacher writes key phrases on the board and asks students to note answers in their books.

Let us Think — A. (p.95): teacher poses question 3 ('How did the Panchayat solve the problem?') and question 4 ('What was the final judgment?'). Students discuss in pairs, then share answers; teacher corrects and consolidates on the board.
Students write answers to all four questions independently in their notebooks, using the board phrases as support. Teacher circulates and gives brief formative feedback.
Quick whole-class check: teacher reads each answer aloud and students confirm or correct their written responses.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full narrative together, students can now locate evidence for each answer in the text. A common slip is to say the Panchayat simply 'gave the water to the farmer' — guide students to articulate the logical argument: if the water belongs to the neighbour, he must remove it from the farmer's well.

periods.activity_title: Think, Discuss and Speak: Fairness in Disputes

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.95, pp.98–99): discuss Panchayat fairness, a shared-box conflict, and identify who said which line.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.95): teacher poses question B.1 — 'Do you think the Panchayat's decision was correct?' Students think for one minute alone, then share their reasons with a partner. Two or three pairs share with the class; teacher records key reasoning words on the board (fair, wise, clever).

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.95): teacher poses question B.2 — the painting-box conflict between Radha and Sita. Students discuss in small groups of three, deciding how they would be fair to both friends. Each group nominates a speaker to share their solution.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.95): teacher reads the three dialogue lines aloud — 'I sold only the well, not the water'; 'Remove the water or use it all up immediately'; 'He is not letting me take the water.' Students identify who said each line to whom, justifying with reference to the story.

Let us Speak (pp.98–99): students look at the four sequential pictures showing a neighbour quarrel. In small groups they predict the ending and one student from each group narrates the group's predicted ending to the class.
Teacher draws the discussion to a close by asking: 'What one word describes how a good Panchayat makes decisions?' Students call out answers; teacher ends on 'fairness'.

periods.teacher_notes: The painting-box scenario (question B.2) is designed to connect the narrative's lesson of fairness to the students' own classroom experience — let the conversation run naturally and avoid pushing a single 'correct' solution. For the picture sequence on pp.98–99, accept any logically consistent ending; the point is fluent oral narration.

periods.activity_title: Let us Listen: Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa Passage

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.101): listen to passage on Sri Ramakrishna and answer five multiple-choice questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher tells students they will listen to a short passage about a wise and kind man from West Bengal. Students are asked to close their textbooks and listen carefully for three key facts: where he was born, who his famous student was, and what he compared religions to.
Let us Listen (p.101): teacher reads the passage on Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa aloud at a natural pace, then reads it a second time slightly more slowly. Students listen with books closed.
Let us Listen (p.101): teacher reads the passage a third time. Students may now open textbooks to the question page (p.101) and note key words as they listen.

Let us Listen (p.101): teacher reads each of the five multiple-choice questions aloud one at a time. Students discuss each question briefly with a neighbour (one minute per question) and circle their chosen option. Teacher then reveals the correct answer after all have chosen.

Whole-class debrief: teacher asks students to explain in one sentence why Sri Ramakrishna compared religions to rivers. Students share; teacher confirms against the passage and notes the idea of unity on the board.
Teacher poses a closing oral question: 'What quality do Naren's teacher and the Panchayat chief share?' Students call out answers freely to close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Repeat the passage three times as NCF guidance recommends for listening at this stage — the first read builds global understanding, the second attends to detail, and the third supports answer selection. Students often confuse Naren with another historical figure; make clear during debrief that Naren grew up to become Swami Vivekananda.

periods.activity_title: Let us Learn: Vocabulary Matching and Prepositions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.96): match six story words with their meanings.
Let us Learn — B. (pp.96–97): fill blanks with correct prepositions from a given list.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (p.97): rearrange five events about Sam's forest walk in the correct sequence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the six words — prospered, cunning, worried, summon, adamant, judgment — on the board. Students try to recall where each word appeared in the narrative and offer a meaning guess before the matching exercise begins.

Let us Learn — A. (p.96): students work individually to match each word to its meaning. Teacher then calls on students to share their matches; the class confirms or corrects each one together, and students note correct pairs in their books.

Teacher introduces prepositions briefly using two of the story sentences from the board, asking: 'Which small word tells us where or when something happened?' Students identify 'under the banyan tree' and 'to the village chief' as examples.

Let us Learn — B. (pp.96–97): teacher reads each sentence aloud and students choose the correct preposition from the given list (in, at, by, after, before, under, with, to, for). Students fill in their books; after every three sentences, the class checks answers together.

Teacher sets the homework task: students will rearrange five events about Sam's walk (Let us Learn — C., p.97) in the correct order in their notebooks. Teacher reads the five events aloud once so students are familiar with them.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary in task A — prospered, adamant, summon — appears directly in the Panchayat story, so encourage students to recall the scene each word belongs to rather than treating it as an isolated list. For the prepositions in task B, sentences 7 and 10 are the trickiest; give extra time on 'under the banyan tree' and 'at a later time'.

periods.activity_title: Let us Write: Letter as the Farmer

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (p.100): write a letter as the farmer to a friend about the dispute and Panchayat's decision.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays a simple letter skeleton on the board: salutation, body (what happened, how the Panchayat helped, how you feel now), and closing. The class recalls the story events in order — the purchase, the neighbour's refusal, the Panchayat judgment — and teacher notes three bullet points on the board as content prompts.

Teacher writes an opening paragraph on the board as a model, thinking aloud: 'My dear friend, Something happened last week which I want to tell you. I wanted to buy a well…' Teacher pauses to ask students what the farmer would say next, incorporating their suggestions into the model.

Let us Write — A. (p.100): students write their own letter independently in their notebooks, beginning with the given opening and continuing through the dispute and the Panchayat's clever judgment. Teacher circulates, offering quiet formative feedback on sequence and voice.

Peer response: students swap notebooks with a partner. The partner checks that the letter includes at least three key events and that the farmer's feelings are expressed. Partners give one verbal suggestion for improvement.
Two or three students read their letters aloud to the class. Teacher acknowledges letters that capture the farmer's relief and the Panchayat's wisdom particularly well.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often retell events without adopting the farmer's first-person voice — during the modelled writing, emphasise words like 'I was upset' and 'I felt relieved' to anchor the personal perspective. Keep the target length realistic: three short paragraphs covering the purchase, the dispute, and the resolution are sufficient for Grade V.

periods.activity_title: Let us Write: The '-less' Suffix and New Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — B. (p.100): add suffix '-less' to five words, then write sentences using each new word.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'priceless' on the board and asks: 'What does the story tell us about water?' Students recall the story context. Teacher explains the suffix '-less' means 'without', and invites students to try: 'If something is priceless, it is without…?' — students complete 'a price'.

Let us Write — B. (p.100): teacher writes all five base words (use, care, hope, fear, colour) on the board. Students add '-less' to each word, check the spelling together as a class, and write the five new words in their notebooks.

Students write one original sentence for each of the five '-less' words in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, reading sentences and suggesting improvements — for example, prompting context: 'Can you write a sentence about the cunning neighbour being careless with his honesty?'
Students share sentences in a round-robin: each student reads one sentence aloud. Class gives a quiet thumbs-up if the new word is used correctly in context.
Teacher closes by asking: 'Can you think of one more '-less' word not in the list?' Students call out answers; teacher writes correct suggestions on the board as a brief extension.

periods.teacher_notes: The suffix task is anchored in the story through the word 'priceless' and the theme of water — keep that thread alive when students write their sentences. Watch for the spelling of 'colourless' (British spelling with 'u'); accept both spellings and note the variation without penalising either.

periods.activity_title: Let us Do: The Neem Tree Passage and Spot the Difference

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (p.103): read the Neem Tree passage and answer seven comprehension questions.
Let us Do — B. (p.104): spot and write 11 differences between two near-identical pictures.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do — A. (p.103): teacher reads the Neem Tree passage aloud once while students follow in their books. Brief discussion: 'Have you seen a neem tree? What do you notice about it?' Students share one observation each.

Let us Do — A. (p.103): students answer questions 1–5 (where neem trees grow, why it is called magic, effect of burning leaves, why leaves are put in storage, how twigs are used) in their notebooks independently. Teacher circulates and gives quiet support.

Let us Do — A. (p.103): class checks answers to questions 1–5 together, then tackles questions 6 and 7 (vocabulary: 'disappear' and 'a short stick') as a group. Teacher confirms 'vanish' and 'twig' and explains briefly how to locate meaning from context.

Let us Do — B. (p.104): students work in pairs, each pair looking carefully at the two pictures. Partners take turns pointing out a difference while the other records it in writing in their notebook. Teacher circulates and encourages pairs who are stuck to look at small details (colours, objects, number of items).
Quick share-out: pairs call out one difference each in rapid succession. Teacher tallies how many the class found collectively and invites any pair that found all eleven to share their final few.

periods.teacher_notes: The Neem Tree passage extends the chapter's theme of natural resources and community wisdom — draw a brief connection for students: just as the Panchayat valued the well's water, communities value the neem tree for its everyday uses. For the spot-the-difference task, encourage pairs to work systematically from top to bottom rather than scanning randomly.

items.source_context: Farmer buys well; neighbour refuses water access; Panchayat delivers clever judgment punishing dishonesty.
items.item_stem: Why did the cunning neighbour refuse to let the farmer use the water from the well after the sale?

options.label: A
options.text: He argued the Panchayat had not approved the sale.

options.label: B
options.text: He believed the farmer already had enough water from his other fields.

options.label: C
options.text: He claimed he had sold only the well structure, not the water inside it.

options.label: D
options.text: He said the farmer had not paid the full price for the well.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Students choosing this may have confused the sale dispute with a payment dispute, missing the neighbour's specific verbal trick.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misreading that introduces the Panchayat into the cause of the dispute rather than its resolution.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student has invented a motive not present in the story, confusing the neighbour's cunning with a practical argument.

items.source_lo: Student locates and explains key events and character motivations using a narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Farmer buys well; neighbour refuses water access; Panchayat delivers clever judgment punishing dishonesty.
items.item_stem: The Panchayat gave a clever judgment to outwit the cunning neighbour. In two or three sentences, explain what the judgment was and why it worked against the neighbour.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The Panchayat ruled that since the neighbour claimed the water was his, he had no right to store it inside someone else's well and must remove or use it immediately. Because removing all the water from a well is impossible, the neighbour was trapped by his own argument and the water effectively passed to the farmer. The neighbour was outwitted, fined, and forced to apologise.

items.item_stem: Listen as your teacher reads the passage about Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa (Textbook p.101). Then answer: Where did Sri Ramakrishna live, and what did he compare all religions to?

options.text: Sri Ramakrishna compared all religions to stars in the sky.
Sri Ramakrishna lived a life of great luxury and wealth.
Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa lived in a small village in West Bengal.
The boy named Naren later became known as Swami Vivekananda.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false — he compared religions to rivers, not stars. Statement 4 is false — he lived a simple life, wearing plain clothes and eating very little.
